query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy, the absence of Co reduces local lattice distortion and alters the balance of solute–dislocation interactions. This lowers the intrinsic lattice friction at room temperature but enhances dislocation inertial effects at cryogenic temperatures and reduces the dynamic solute pinning (PL effect) at elevated temperatures. Consequently, the alloy will show a steeper increase in CRSS at low temperatures due to pronounced dislocation inertia and a smaller high‐temperature CRSS increment with less serrated flow compared to the Co‐containing baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, water-quenched, equiatomic FCC single crystals of the Co-free alloy FeNiCrMn prepared by Bridgman or optical floating-zone methods, followed by annealing (e.g., 168 h at 1273–1473 K) and machining into [1̄23]-oriented compression specimens.
generation.intervention: Perform uniaxial compression tests on the [1̄23]-oriented crystals across a broad temperature range (from cryogenic ~9 K up to 1373 K) and include controlled strain-rate jumps (ranging from 1×10^-4 to 1×10^-2 s^-1) during low-hardening deformation. Complement these mechanical tests with TEM characterization of dislocation structures in specimens deformed at selected high temperatures.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in compression at an engineering strain rate of 1×10^-4 s^-1 (with intermittent strain-rate jumps) over a temperature range spanning cryogenic (<77 K), room, and high-temperature (above ~700 K) regimes, excluding temperature ranges where extreme inertial dynamics or extrinsic instabilities dominate.
generation.structural_mediator: The locally reduced lattice distortion (quantified by a lower mean-square atomic displacement relative to Co-containing alloys) alters the dislocation glide-resistance landscape. At low temperatures, the lower lattice friction accentuates the role of inertial dislocation motion, while at high temperatures, the effectiveness of dynamic solute pinning by Mn and Fe (which are now the dominant solute atoms) is diminished relative to alloys containing Co.
generation.mechanism: At cryogenic temperatures, with reduced phonon damping, the lower lattice friction enhances dislocation inertial motion, resulting in a steeper increase in the critical resolved shear stress (CRSS). Conversely, at elevated temperatures, the diffusion of Fe and Mn solutes produces a dynamic, yet less effective, dislocation pinning (a Portevin–Le Chatelier effect) that leads to milder CRSS enhancement and reduced serrated flow compared to the Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Co-containing equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (which serves as the baseline), the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is predicted to exhibit (1) a sharper increase in CRSS upon cooling below room temperature—with the CRSS increase becoming less steep below ~77 K due to dislocation inertia—and (2) a smaller CRSS increment and less-pronounced serrated flow features when heated into the diffusion-active regime above ~700 K.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the mechanical response (CRSS values, strain-rate sensitivity, and serrated flow features) obtained from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi under identical processing and testing conditions, particularly the room-temperature CRSS and intermediate-temperature plateau prior to high-temperature PL effects.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single-phase, equiatomic FCC HEAs processed into [1̄23]-oriented single crystals and tested in compression over the temperature range where conventional thermal activation controls dislocation glide (above the alloy-specific inertial cutoff near ~60–77 K and below the onset of extraneous instabilities beyond ~1373 K). It is most relevant when comparing chemically similar systems that differ primarily by the absence or presence of Co.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by trends observed in related Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys, the specific quantitative differences in CRSS increments and serration magnitudes between the Co-free and Co-containing variants remain uncertain due to potential variations in short-range order and magnetic interactions not captured by nonmagnetic calculations.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct temperature- and strain-rate-dependent compression tests on both Co-free FeNiCrMn single crystals and Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi single crystals. Measure the CRSS from 0.2% offset yield stress along with strain-rate sensitivity and stress–strain serrations across the temperature range from cryogenic to high temperatures. Use TEM to observe dislocation structures post-deformation at room and high temperatures.
measurements: Temperature-dependent CRSS from 0.2% offset yield stress with slip-trace verification
Strain-rate sensitivity from controlled rate-jump tests to capture inertial onset effects at low temperatures
High-temperature stress–strain curves to identify the magnitude of the PL effect and serrated flow characteristics
TEM observations of dislocation configurations and partial-dislocation separations at room and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy does not exhibit a steeper increase in CRSS at cryogenic temperatures relative to the Co-containing baseline, or if the high-temperature CRSS increment and serration effects are comparable to or more pronounced than in the Co-containing alloy, then the hypothesis is rejected.
